# Help people understand and revise a plan

People who plan work see when each task happens and how the tasks depend on each other.
They change the plan when their situation changes, see what the change does to the rest
of it, and keep the plan in their own hands.

This repository is also a worked example of specspec: a reader can follow how the app's
specification and code came about, stage by stage.

# Make timing readable

A person reads from the plan when each task starts and ends and how the tasks lie in
time relative to each other, as a picture and as text.

# Show tasks as bars on a shared calendar axis

Each task is a row with its name and a bar from its start to its end, on one calendar
axis shared by all tasks. A table lists the same start and end dates as text. Long plans
scroll sideways inside the chart, and the controls work from the keyboard.

# Validate input and render project text literally

Names and imported data are treated as text: the browser shows them through textContent
and ordinary native controls. A changed plan is validated as a whole before it replaces
the saved plan. When input is invalid, the app says what to correct and keeps the valid
saved work and the draft being edited.

# Record every stage as specification before code

Each stage of the app is planned in this graph and committed before its code is written.
Planning commits are titled `Agent specspec changes:`. When the app changes direction,
the nodes that no longer apply are deleted, the commit message says why, and they stay
readable in the earlier commits.

# Plan a business portfolio

A manager sees several business projects together, with every task assigned to one
project. The portfolio appears as one calendar and one task table.

# Forecast business-day prerequisite timing

The app forecasts each task's start and end from its duration in working days and from
the tasks that have to finish before it. Working days are Monday to Friday. Every task
shows its forecast dates.

# Identify responsible team members

Every task names the team member responsible for it, and the name appears next to the
task's project and dates.

# Keep one person from being booked twice

The schedule delays a task when its team member is already planned on another task on
the same days.

# Summarize portfolio completion

Each project shows how far it is, next to its tasks. The summary says how it is
calculated, and the tasks and their progress values stay visible beside it.

# Let team members share plans through accounts

Team members sign in and open the same plans. Who may see and change a plan is
controlled per account, and the plans are stored in one place for everyone.

# Read project and portfolio finish timing

Every project and the whole portfolio show the date on which they are forecast to
finish, in the calendar and in the project summaries. The app says that these dates are
forecasts from durations and prerequisites.

# Use whole UTC weekdays for the portfolio forecast

Dates are real ISO calendar dates, read as whole days in UTC. A project start on a
weekend moves to the next Monday. Tasks are processed in prerequisite order: a task
starts on the later of the project start and the next weekday after its last
prerequisite ends, and its duration counts its first workday. A plan is valid when task
IDs are unique and nonempty, durations are 1 to 100 workdays, progress is a finite
number from 0 to 100 and every prerequisite names an existing task without forming a
cycle. The forecast returns the tasks in the order they were entered and leaves the
entered data unchanged. The calendar consists of the weekdays Monday to Friday.

# Serve shared plans over HTTP from a relational store

A web service holds the shared plans in a relational database and serves them over HTTP.
Account permissions, hosting and the handling of personal data are open.

# Calculate inspectable project rollups

Tasks are grouped by project. A project's finish is the latest end date of its tasks,
and its completion is the rounded mean of its tasks' completion values, each task
counting the same. The summary shows the number of tasks, and the task rows stay
visible, so the figures can be checked by hand.

# Delay overlapping work in one greedy pass

After the dependency forecast, the scheduler goes through the tasks in order and moves a
task to the first days on which its team member is free. The order of the pass, the
handling of ties and each member's own calendar are open.

# Compute the local portfolio forecast and rollups

`model.js` implements the validated UTC weekday forecast with prerequisites and the
project rollups for finish date and mean progress, over local demo data. The responsible
team member is a displayed field. `test/model.test.cjs` covers weekend boundaries,
independence from task order, malformed data, cycles, missing references and the rollup
figures. Scheduling around a person's other tasks and shared accounts have no code at
this stage.

# Render a local read-only portfolio timeline

Local classic scripts, native text and CSS show the project summaries, a row per task
with responsible member, dates and progress, and bars on one calendar axis. `index.html`
opens directly or from a local static server and shows the demo plan bundled with the
prototype. A syntax check and the model tests cover this stage; the page has no browser
test.

# Plan one personal renovation

One person plans a home renovation: tasks with dates and priorities on a readable
timeline. The whole plan belongs to that person and lives in their browser and in a JSON
file.

# Let the person choose every task date

The person enters the start and the end date of each task. Saving a task changes that
task's dates and leaves all other tasks as they are. The timeline and the table show
both dates, each counted as part of the task.

# Include every calendar day in personal planning

Weekends are drawn as ordinary days, because personal work happens on any day. A task
counts its start day and its end day.

# Identify personal task priorities

A task is marked low, normal or high. The priority appears next to the task's dates in
the timeline and in the table.

# Keep a portable validated JSON plan

The plan is exported to and imported from a documented, versioned JSON file that the
person keeps. An import is validated and shown as a preview that names what a conversion
changes or loses; it replaces the current plan when the person confirms. Export writes
the saved valid plan.

# Save valid work in this browser

Valid edits are saved automatically in the browser's local storage when it is available.
When it is unavailable or fails, the app says that the plan lives for this session only
and points to the JSON export, which saves the work independently of the browser.

# Give personal tasks independent date ranges

Every task has a date range of its own, chosen by hand. Editing one task leaves the
ranges of all others as they are, so the timeline shows exactly the dates the person
entered.

# Validate inclusive manual UTC calendar ranges

Dates are real ISO dates between 2000-01-01 and 2100-12-31, read as whole days in UTC. A
task ends on or after the day it starts and spans end minus start plus one days, so a
one-day task and a weekend task are valid. All tasks together fit into at most 730
calendar days. Validating a changed plan keeps the entered ranges and the order of the
tasks.

# Autosave through localStorage with protected original bytes

The validated plan is saved in the browser's localStorage under a stable local origin.
When storage fails, the app keeps working in memory and shows that the plan is
session-only and how to export it. Saved bytes that cannot be read stay as they are
until the person resets them or replaces them through a previewed import. Browser
storage depends on the browser, the origin and its storage settings; the exported file
is the copy the person controls.

# Define version-one manual-plan JSON

A `version: 1` file holds a title and tasks. A task has a unique ID, a title, ISO start
and end dates and a priority of low, normal or high. A plan has at most 100 tasks; IDs
are 1 to 40 letters, digits, `_` or `-`; names and the title are trimmed, nonempty and
at most 120 characters. An import is applied when its dates are real and within bounds,
every range is ordered and the chart spans at most 730 days. The validated plan is a
normalized copy with the tasks in the order they were entered.

# Validate independent inclusive personal dates

`model.js` normalizes a version-one title and its tasks, validates IDs, priorities,
calendar ranges and the bounds of the chart, and computes inclusive spans. Input data
stays unchanged and saved ranges stay independent of each other. The model tests cover
same-day and weekend ranges, independence from task order, a JSON round trip and invalid
data. `history/personal-v1.json` is the exported demo plan, kept as a sample of the
portable format.

# Edit and store a local personal timeline

Native forms create, edit and delete tasks with their date ranges and priorities. A
chart that scrolls sideways and a date table show every calendar day. Validated saves
are stored locally; when storing or loading fails, the plan stays session-only and the
stored bytes stay protected until reset. Export downloads a JSON file, and a confirmed
import is validated before it replaces the plan. Project strings are set through
textContent. A syntax check and the model tests cover this stage; browser storage and
interaction have no automated test at this stage.

# Plan one makerspace workshop

A makerspace organizes one workshop: tasks with durations, prerequisites and earliest
dates, and a baseline to compare a what-if against. The plan stays local and portable.

# Forecast dates from whole workday durations

Each task has a duration in whole working days, Monday to Friday. The app calculates
every task's forecast start and end and recalculates the affected dates after each valid
edit. It presents the dates as estimates that follow from the calendar and the
prerequisites.

# Respect finish-to-start prerequisites

A task names other existing tasks as prerequisites, without cycles, and starts after all
of them have finished. A link to a missing task or a cycle is reported before the change
is applied, and the saved valid plan stays.

# Respect project and task earliest-start bounds

The project start and an optional earliest date per task are lower bounds for the
forecast. A bound on a weekend moves to the following Monday. The app presents the
calculated dates as forecasts that respect these bounds and the prerequisites.

# Use an explicit Monday–Friday workshop calendar

Durations count whole working days from Monday to Friday. The calendar axis shows every
day and shades the weekends. The forecast follows from working-day durations and
prerequisites alone.

# Compare a what-if with a deliberately captured baseline

On request the app captures the complete saved plan as a baseline. The person then edits
the plan and sees the current dates beside the baseline's, in the chart and as text.
Ordinary edits leave the baseline as captured; replacing or clearing it is an explicit
action.

# Edit a validated complete workshop task set

Tasks are added, selected, edited and removed through accessible native forms. A change
is saved after its durations, bounds and prerequisites have been validated. A task that
others depend on can be removed once the person has changed those tasks' links. An
invalid edit or a cancelled navigation keeps the draft and the saved valid plan.

# Preview personal-file conversion before replacing work

A version-one file from the personal planner can be imported: the app shows a preview of
the workshop plan it would become and explains which dates and priorities are lost and
that dates turn into weekday forecasts. The plan is replaced when the person presses
Apply; previewing or cancelling leaves the saved work and the browser storage as they
are.

# Calculate bounded UTC weekday DAG forecasts iteratively

Dates are whole days in UTC, and tasks are processed iteratively in prerequisite order.
A task starts on the latest of the normalized project start, its own normalized earliest
date and the next weekday after each prerequisite's end; it ends duration minus one
workdays after its start. The result lists the tasks in saved order and leaves the input
unchanged. A plan is valid with up to 100 tasks, durations of 1 to 60 whole workdays,
real ISO dates from 2000 to 2100, unique task IDs of 1 to 40 letters, digits, `_` or
`-`, trimmed titles and names of 1 to 120 characters, and prerequisites that are
distinct existing tasks other than the task itself. A cyclic or invalid plan is
rejected. The earliest date may be null or empty. The current plan and the baseline
together fit an axis of at most 730 calendar days, counted inclusively over the
normalized starts and all forecast rows. The model is a small deterministic dependency
forecast.

# Store an explicit deep baseline and compare on a common axis

On request the app stores a normalized copy of the complete saved plan, and later edits
leave that copy as it is. The current plan and the baseline are forecast independently
and drawn on the same bounded calendar axis: the current tasks in their order, followed
by tasks that exist only in the baseline. The text view gives start, end and the
difference of the finish dates in calendar days. A task found only in the baseline stays
visible as removed, a task found only in the current plan is marked Added, and a missing
baseline date leaves the comparison empty. Replacing and clearing the baseline are
explicit actions, and validation leaves both snapshots as they are.

# Define version-two workshop JSON and previewed conversion

A `version: 2` file holds title, start, tasks and an optional complete baseline. A task
has id, title, duration, earliest and dependsOn. Loading normalizes copies of the fields
and validates both forecasts and their common axis; saving serializes the saved plan.
The import preview accepts up to one million characters of pasted text and files of up
to one million bytes. Apply replaces the saved work and the browser storage after
confirmation; Cancel keeps both. A valid version-one range becomes a duration of the
weekdays it contains, at least one; the old start becomes the task's earliest date,
prerequisites and the baseline start empty, and the project starts at the earliest task
start, or on 2026-04-06 for an empty plan. The version-one priority is read and reported
as dropped. The preview warns that a hand-entered end becomes a forecast from the
duration and that a range lying on a weekend moves to a workday. Stored version-one
bytes stay protected until preview and Apply, or reset.

# Use local classic scripts, native forms and a DOM calendar

The app consists of local classic scripts without dependencies, sets project strings
through textContent and uses native controls. It starts from local files or from a
stable local static origin; the static origin gives predictable browser storage, and a
start from files that cannot store shows the session-only guidance. The calendar scrolls
sideways, shades weekends, draws current and baseline bars differently and comes with a
text table of dates. Scrolling stays inside the chart and the table, and the form and
the caret stay in place when the window is resized. Pasted or loaded JSON is previewed
apart from the saved data, a file read that has been overtaken is cancelled, and the app
asks before unsaved task or settings input is discarded. Prerequisites in the app
describe the schedule; links in this graph say why a node is there.

# Calculate workshop forecasts, baseline snapshots and JSON previews

`model.js` implements the iterative UTC weekday forecast over prerequisites, bounded
normalization, copied baselines that later edits leave unchanged, rows for the current
plan and the baseline, and their differences in calendar days. Saving a task validates
the whole changed plan; removing a task validates that no other task still refers to it.
Import returns a validated version-two preview or the warnings of a version-one
conversion. The model tests cover seeded dependency graphs against an independent
reference, deep bounded graphs, weekend, daylight-saving and leap-year dates, invalid
and cyclic input, unchanged input and baseline, and the archived personal JSON file. The
model is pure and deterministic over local data.

# Edit and persist a native local workshop calendar

`app.js`, the local markup and the styles implement current and baseline bars, the date
table, weekend shading, editable prerequisites and the explicit capture, replacement and
clearing of the baseline. Valid edits are saved automatically. Corrupt or version-one
bytes in storage can be downloaded and stay protected until Apply or reset. An import
preview and a cancelled or overtaken file read leave the saved work as it is. A failed
draft and the caret stay in place through invalid edits and resizing. Project strings
are set through textContent. Tests in a real browser cover forecasts, baselines, cyclic
drafts, safe removal of tasks, literal markup, downloads and uploads, conversion preview
with Cancel and Apply, reload, protected and denied storage, and a start directly from
the file. The model tests and the browser tests are repeatable checks of this local
planner.

# Receipts and a stage ledger for the recorded history

`history/cli.jsonl` holds the specspec commands that built this graph, with their actual
results. `history/revisions.json` names the planning commit and the code commit of every
stage and the receipts that end them. Planning commits come before the code they plan,
and the commit of each redirect says what was deleted and why; the deleted nodes stay
readable in the commits before it.

# Receipts, a stage ledger and a verifier for the recorded history

`history/cli.jsonl` holds the specspec commands that built this graph, with their actual
results. `history/revisions.json` names the planning commit and the code commit of every
stage and the receipts that end them. Planning commits come before the code they plan,
and the commit of each redirect says what was deleted and why; the deleted nodes stay
readable in the commits before it. `history/verify.py` checks every commit and tag of
this history: valid graphs in the current format, the exact staged state, the receipts
against the graphs, the order of planning and code, what each redirect removed, the
source links and the model tests of every stage. `STORY.md` tells the product briefs as
a fictional dialogue, and `README.md` and `history/WALKTHROUGH.md` explain how to open
and compare the stages.
